name: Strangford langoustines
story: Spring creel season is in full swing. Firm, sweet, unstressed. Pulled by hand from the lough floor — minutes from the boat to the harbour wall.

name: Strangford Lough oysters
story: Rope-grown on the lough, deeply flavoured by the exceptional water quality of a designated European Marine Site. Clean, briny, full of place.

name: Abernethy spring butter
story: Hand-churned from single-farm cream out of the Lagan Valley. Spring cream is the richest of the year — the dulse and sea salt variety is the one to seek out.

name: Wild garlic
story: A brief, intense window through March and April when the County Down woodlands go magnificently green and pungent. Forage the edges, mind the bluebells, get there before it flowers — by mid-May it's over for the year.

name: Comber Earlies
story: PGI-protected new potatoes from the heavy clay soils around Comber. First diggings expected late May. Boil for ten minutes, smear with butter, salt heavily.

name: Lobster
story: Down coast lobster from the Kilkeel and Portavogie fleets. Sweet, dense flesh — the absolute peak of Irish summer eating. Boil briefly, butter generously.

name: Asparagus
story: A short, glorious window. From small County Down market gardens — cut that morning, on the plate that evening. The shorter the gap, the sweeter the spear.

name: Strawberries
story: The County Down soft fruit season runs through summer with the peak in July. Finlay's Place opens for pick-your-own — eat them warm from the sun, the day they're picked. Nothing in any supermarket comes close.

name: Brown crab
story: Crab season builds through summer and peaks in early autumn. Creel-caught brown crab off the Co Down coast — sweet white meat, rich brown meat, both at their best from August. Landed and supplied through East Coast Seafoods at Ballyhornan.

name: Lough Neagh pollan
story: Endemic to Lough Neagh — a glacial relict species found in only a handful of Irish loughs. Eaten on the lough shore, exported to Switzerland, almost invisible elsewhere.

name: Lough Neagh eels
story: PGI-protected, caught by the Lough Neagh Fishermen's Co-operative at Toomebridge. Most are exported to Holland to be smoked. The Sargasso Sea to the lough and back — the great migration story of Ulster food.

name: Heather honey
story: Late summer brings the heather harvest from the Mournes and the higher ground. Dark, thick, intensely floral. The flagship Ulster honey of the year.

name: Heritage apples
story: Armagh is the orchard county of Ireland. Bramley for cooking, heritage varieties for eating — the harvest builds through September and runs into winter storage.

name: Venison
story: Wild and farmed venison through the colder months — Finnebrogue Estate near Downpatrick is the County Down anchor. Lean, deeply flavoured, the proper winter meat.

name: Elderflower
story: The hedgerows along quiet County Down lanes are about to burst into creamy elderflower clusters. A six-week window from late May for cordial, fritters and elderflower champagne. Pick on a dry sunny morning — the scent doesn't keep.

name: Samphire
story: Salt-tolerant marsh samphire on the muddy shores of Strangford Lough and the Down coast. Cut with scissors above the woody base. Blanch briefly, butter generously, eat with anything from the sea.

name: Sea spinach
story: Wild sea beet on the upper shore — leafier and more interesting than its cultivated cousin. Look for it on the strandlines from Killyleagh round to Ballyhalbert. Wilts down to nothing, so pick a proper bag.

name: Wild blackberries
story: The August hedgerow gift. Every back lane in County Down delivers them — best the day after a warm spell, picked low to avoid the dog walkers. Fold into apple crumbles, make jam, freeze flat on a tray for winter.

name: Chanterelles
story: Golden chanterelles under the spruce in the Mournes and Tollymore in late summer. Apricot-scented, peppery, the finest wild mushroom that grows in Ulster. Only forage what you can identify with certainty.

name: Sloes
story: Blackthorn fruits along the lanes, ready after the first frost. Tart and astringent raw — they exist to be steeped in gin with sugar and patience. Pick October, drink by Christmas.
